title: Episode 97: The Gilded Age of Newport: The Astors, Vanderbilts, and Summer Palaces
description:
Between 1880 and 1914, America's ultra-wealthy industrial dynasties transformed the quiet seaport of Newport, Rhode Island, into a dazzling summer playground, erecting fifty-room marble 'cottages' and waging ruthless high-society warfare on Bellevue Avenue.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the glittering, ruthless, and breathtaking world of late nineteenth-century high society in Newport, Rhode Island: the Gilded Age of America's summer capital. Along the windswept cliffs of Bellevue Avenue, industrial robber barons, railroad titans, and banking dynasts—the Vanderbilts, Astors, Goelets, and Morgans—spent staggering fortunes to outdo one another in an architectural arms race of unprecedented extravagance. Modestly dubbed 'summer cottages,' these monumental Italianate palazzos and French châteaux were home to fifty-course banquets, gold-plated flatware, diamond-studded party favors, and savage social warfare governed by the iron fist of Mrs. Astor. Here is George with the full, glittering spectacle of Newport.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: FROM COLONIAL SEAPORT TO SOCIETY HAVEN
In the eighteenth century, Newport, Rhode Island was one of the premier commercial seaports of British North America, bustling with merchant sailing ships, whale oil refineries, and rum distilleries. But during the American Revolution, British occupation devastated the harbor, destroying hundreds of wharves and driving away its merchant class. For decades, Newport slumbered as a picturesque maritime relic of colonial times, its sea breezes and mild summer climate attracting intellectuals, artists, and wealthy Southern plantation owners who sought refuge from summer heat and malaria.
Following the Civil War, however, the unprecedented economic explosion of American industrialization created staggering fortunes the world had never seen. In New York, Chicago, and Pittsburgh, railroad magnates, oil monopolists, and steel barons accumulated wealth that dwarfed European aristocracies. Seeking a refined, exclusive sanctuary to escape the sweltering heat, industrial grime, and democratic crowds of Manhattan, New York's high society turned their eyes toward the oceanfront bluffs of Aquidneck Island.
Between eighteen eighty and nineteen fourteen, the quiet coastal town was transformed into the undisputed summer capital of the Gilded Age. Along Bellevue Avenue and the dramatic rocky shoreline of the Cliff Walk, America's newly minted plutocrats purchased farmland and fishing pastures, initiating an architectural and social competition of breathtaking extravagance. The tranquil salt marshes and dramatic granite cliffs of Aquidneck Island provided an incomparable natural canvas for Europe's grandest architectural styles.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE QUEEN OF HIGH SOCIETY: MRS. ASTOR AND THE FOUR HUNDRED
At the apex of this dazzling social pyramid stood one supreme, unchallenged sovereign: Caroline Webster Schermerhorn Astor, known universally to the world simply as 'The Mrs. Astor.' Descended from old Dutch patrician stock and married to William Backhouse Astor Jr.—heir to the immense fur and New York real estate fortune—Mrs. Astor ruled American high society with an iron fist of etiquette and exclusionary snobbery.
Assisting Mrs. Astor was Ward McAllister, an eccentric, self-appointed social arbiter who famously coined the term 'The Four Hundred.' McAllister declared that there were only four hundred people in fashionable New York and Newport who truly mattered—conveniently, the exact number of guests who could fit comfortably into Mrs. Astor's Manhattan ballroom without causing an undignified crush. To be recognized by Mrs. Astor, to receive her engraved calling card or an invitation to her summer ball at her Newport estate, Beechwood, was the ultimate validation of social legitimacy.
For newly rich industrialists and railroad tycoons, wealth alone was insufficient to breach the fortress of the old-money Knickerbocker elite. Mrs. Astor viewed these 'nouveaux riches' with patrician disdain, requiring aspiring dynasties to endure years of humiliating social vetting before granting them entrance to the sacred inner circle. This rigid social blockade catalyzed an architectural explosion as ambitious outsiders resolved to build monuments so magnificent that even Mrs. Astor could not ignore them. Mrs. Astor's imperious social decrees dictated everything from the length of ball gowns to acceptable family pedigrees throughout nineteenth-century America.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE BREAKERS: THE VANDERBILT TEMPLE OF POWER
Leading the assault on the old-money citadel was the formidable Vanderbilt dynasty. Commodore Cornelius Vanderbilt had amassed the greatest fortune in America through steamships and the New York Central Railroad, but his rough-hewn manners had kept the family excluded from polite society. His grandchildren, armed with hundreds of millions of dollars and an insatiable desire for social coronation, resolved to conquer Newport by outbuilding everyone on earth.
In eighteen ninety-three, following a fire that destroyed his previous wooden summer home, Cornelius Vanderbilt the Second commissioned America's preeminent Gilded Age architect, Richard Morris Hunt, to design the ultimate statement of dynastic supremacy: The Breakers. Inspired by the sixteenth-century Renaissance palaces of Genoa and Turin, Hunt constructed a colossal seventy-room, five-story Italianate palazzo encompassing over one hundred and twenty-five thousand square feet of floor space.
Constructed entirely of Indiana limestone, Caen stone from France, and fireproof masonry, The Breakers was a marvel of architectural grandeur and engineering sophistication. Inside, visitors entered a soaring two-story Great Hall forty-five feet high, illuminated by massive wrought-iron and bronze chandeliers. Master craftsmen from Paris and Rome were imported to carve rare Numidian and Brecce marbles, gild ceilings with pure twenty-two-karat gold leaf, and install mosaic vaulted ceilings made of millions of hand-cut tiles. Yet despite possessing fifty-four guest and family rooms, thirty-three staff bedrooms, and a dining room with twelve solid alabaster columns, the Vanderbilts referred to this monumental palace with supreme understatement as their 'summer cottage'—occupied for barely six to eight weeks every July and August. Over five hundred European artisans lived on the estate during construction, hand-carving Caen stone fireplaces and laying intricate mosaic floors.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: MARBLE HOUSE: ALVA VANDERBILT'S SOCIAL TRIUMPH
Just down Bellevue Avenue stood an even more audacious monument to social ambition: Marble House, built by Cornelius's brother, William Kissam Vanderbilt, as a thirty-ninth birthday gift for his relentlessly ambitious wife, Alva Erskine Smith Vanderbilt. Alva was a brilliant, iron-willed social strategist who was determined to force Mrs. Astor and the Knickerbocker elite to bow before the Vanderbilt name.
Completed in eighteen ninety-two at the staggering cost of eleven million dollars—equivalent to over three hundred and fifty million dollars today—Marble House incorporated five hundred thousand cubic feet of imported white Italian marble. Hunt designed the temple in the style of the Petit Trianon at Versailles, featuring four monumental Corinthian columns fronting the ocean and an opulent Gold Room whose walls were covered in intricately carved, gold-leaf-gilded bas-relief panels depicting Greek mythological legends.
Alva used Marble House as an instrument of social warfare. In eighteen ninety-five, she engineered the ultimate dynastic marriage between her eighteen-year-old daughter, Consuelo Vanderbilt, and Charles Spencer-Churchill, the ninth Duke of Marlborough. By trading Vanderbilt railroad millions for a British ducal coronet and an ancestral seat at Blenheim Palace, Alva outflanked Mrs. Astor completely. Overnight, the Vanderbilts were no longer merely American millionaires; they were allied with European royalty, forcing every high-society matriarch in Newport to seek invitations to Alva's marble salon. Alva Vanderbilt's audacious coup proved that American railroad wealth could conquer centuries of European aristocratic pedigree at will.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE RITUALS OF EXTRAVAGANCE
Life in Newport during the six-week summer 'season' was governed by an exhausting, rigid schedule of ritualized display and staggering consumption. The day began with private morning strolls or carriage drives along Ocean Drive, followed by formal luncheons that required full afternoon attire. At four o'clock in the afternoon, the sacred ritual of carriage parade commenced: ladies adorned in Parisian couture gowns by the House of Worth were chauffeured along Bellevue Avenue in polished broughams and victorias, leaving engraved calling cards at the marble gates of rivals.
Evenings were consumed by lavish private dinners of eight to twelve courses, prepared by imported French chefs and served on solid silver or gold-plated service by liveried footmen in silk stockings and powdered wigs. Each course was paired with rare vintages from private cellars: Dom Pérignon champagne, Château Lafite, and Rhine wines chilled in silver buckets. After dinner, guests retired to grand ballrooms where full symphony orchestras played waltzes under the glow of thousands of wax candles and electric chandeliers until dawn.
Hosts competed savagely to devise the most bizarre and memorable entertainment. At one famous dinner given by socialite Harry Lehr, a tuxedo-clad chimpanzee named 'Prince Del Drago' was seated at the head of the banquet table as the guest of honor. At another famous party given by Mrs. Stuyvesant Fish, guests were given small silver trowels and invited to dig for buried diamonds, pearls, and sapphires in a tabletop garden of sand. Millions were spent on yachts like J. Pierpont Morgan's Corsair, which rode at anchor in Newport Harbor like private naval flagships. Footmen dressed in knee breeches and powdered wigs stood behind every dinner chair, presenting silver platters in choreographed military unison.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE INVISIBLE ARMY OF SERVANTS
Behind the shimmering façade of gold leaf, champagne, and diamond tiaras stood an invisible, highly disciplined army of domestic servants without whom the palaces of Newport could not function for an hour. A single grand estate like The Breakers or Marble House required a permanent summer staff of forty to sixty servants, recruited from England, Ireland, France, and Sweden, operating under a rigid upstairs-downstairs hierarchy.
Under the command of the English butler and the French housekeeper, footmen, chambermaids, laundresses, scullery maids, and parlor maids worked sixteen-hour days in sweltering basement kitchens and service wings. Servants moved through the cottages via a hidden network of private corridors, spiral staircases, and subterranean tunnels concealed behind mahogany paneling and velvet draperies, ensuring that their labor never disrupted the visual aesthetic of aristocratic leisure.
Laundresses washed, starched, and hand-ironed hundreds of delicate silk dresses and linen shirts daily; footmen polished miles of marble floors and thousands of pieces of silver flatware; and stable grooms attended to dozens of prize carriage horses. While the masters strolled on the lawns overlooking the Atlantic, the men and women in the basements lived on modest wages, observing the unfathomable wealth of their employers with a mixture of awe, exhaustion, and quiet resentment. Without the tireless dawn-to-dusk labor of the liveried servant army, Newport's dazzling social facade would have collapsed within a single afternoon.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SUNSET OF THE GILDED AGE
The dazzling, unsustainable spectacle of Gilded Age Newport could not survive the social and economic revolutions of the early twentieth century. The first blow arrived in nineteen thirteen with the ratification of the Sixteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, establishing the federal income tax, quickly followed by the introduction of inheritance taxes that eroded massive dynastic fortunes. The outbreak of World War I in nineteen fourteen brought an abrupt end to European grand tours and aristocratic marriages, while the Great Depression of nineteen twenty-nine decimated corporate fortunes and altered public tolerance for ostentatious display.
By the nineteen thirties and nineteen forties, the colossal white elephants of Bellevue Avenue had become impossible to maintain. Heating a seventy-room marble palace with coal required thousands of dollars a month, and the pool of trained domestic servants evaporated as modern women sought higher wages and dignity in commercial offices and factories. Many grand estates fell into disrepair, their lawns overgrown with weeds, while others were demolished by developers or sold to institutions for pennies on the dollar.
Yet Newport was saved from total oblivion by the vision of local preservationists who established the Preservation Society of Newport County in nineteen forty-five. Today, The Breakers, Marble House, Rosecliff, and Elms stand preserved as breathtaking architectural museums, welcoming millions of visitors from around the world. They stand as magnificent, haunting monuments to a vanished chapter in American civilization: an era of unbounded ambition, jaw-dropping craftsmanship, and imperial extravagance that will never be seen again. The magnificent preserved cottages remain enduring symbols of an unrepeatable chapter in American industrial and architectural history.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The summer cottages of Newport remain monuments to a vanished world of breathtaking ambition, craftsmanship, and imperial extravagance. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we visit the fear-haunted meetinghouses of Massachusetts for the Salem Witch Trials of sixteen ninety-two.
